title: Electrochemical Reduction of C02 at Intentionally Oxidized Copper Electrodes
abstract: We observed CO2 reduction to CH3OH at various oxidized copper electrodes at 22~ The electrode types included anodized Cu foil, Cu foil thermally oxidized in air, and air-oxidized Cu electrodeposited on anodized or air-oxidized Ti foil. The highest rates to date, 1 • 10 4 mol cm -2 h -1 (geometrical area), were found using anodized Cu in 0.5M KHCO3, pH = 7.6, and -1.9 V (SCE). Faradaic yields for CH3OH depended on the current and reached about 240%. The onset potential for CH3OH formation was near -0.4 V (SCE). Hydrogen gas and small amounts of CO were also formed. A mechanism is proposed involving chemical reduction steps up to HCOad, followed by three hydiogenation steps to CH3OH. Absorption of oxygen by Cure is implied. The stability of p-Cu20 semiconductor films is discussed in terms of breakdown currents d/le to band-to-band tunneling. The major impurities deposited on the Cu electrode during electrolysis are Zn and Fe at several atom percent each. An 8% level of C1 was found, originating from the HC1 etch used to remove the native oxide before thermal oxidation. We have demonstrated electrochemical reduction of aqueous CO2 to methanol at room temperature and ambient pressure using GaAs, InP (1), and Mo (2) electrodes. All these materials have the common property that their surfaces are thermodynamical ly unstable in aqueous solution and are believed to have at least a monolayer of oxygen (sometimes as the oxide phase) present under ordinary electrochemical conditions. We have investigated the Cu20/Cu electrode for its ability to promote the formation of CH3OH. Several reasons for expecting oxidized copper to be active for CH3OH are the following. The Cu/ZnO (3) catalyst is used for the commercial production of methanol from CO and H2. There are new findings regarding the roles of CO2 and ZnO (4). The weak binding of linear CO as found on Cure single crystals means that at practical temperatures, 250~ of operation of Cu/ZnO methanol synthesis reactors, CO would be thermally desorbed from the unoxidized metal. The enhancement of methanol synthesis rates from CO/I-I2 by small amounts of oxidants such as CO2, 02, and water vapor, perhaps by controlling the number of Cu(I) sites, is cited (3) as evidence that oxidized Cu(I) is advantageous in CH3OH synthesis. A possible factor is the stronger binding of CO2 and CO on p-Cu20 and other Cu(I) centers compared to Cure. Changes in the binding of CO brought on by oxidation of Cure may favorably influence its surface hydrogenation to CH3OH. In some previous work (5), we had found that anodized copper foils produced some CH4, CO, and H2, but a major liquid-phase product was indicated in order to bring the products into faradaic balance. Work by Hori et al. (6) on CO2 reduction in 0.5M bicarbonate electrolyte at room temperature using an unintentionally oxidized Cu electrode showed that CH4, HCOO-, and H~ were the dominant products. For example, at -1.6 V vs. SCE, faradaic yields for HCOO-, CH4, C~H4, and H2 were 19, 33, 13, and 31%, respectively. These authors also showed that small amounts of CO and the alcohols C2H5OH and C3H7OH were formed. Formate thus appears to be the major liquid-phase product at unoxidized Cu electrodes. Cooke et al. (7) have investigatged CO~ reduction on perovskites in which the Cu(II) oxidation state is stabilized. They report ethanol and n-propanol formation.
